summary: Defines the MULTIAPPEND extension to IMAP, letting a client upload several messages to a mailbox in a single operation. This speeds up clients that upload many messages, and servers advertise support with a capability name.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of carrying one letter at a time to the mailbox, you can drop off a whole stack at once. This extension lets email programs do that.

questions: how to upload multiple messages with imap
subtitle: Upload a whole batch of messages to an IMAP mailbox with one APPEND command, all or nothing.

tldr.problem: In base IMAP each message is uploaded with its own APPEND command, so a failure part way through leaves the mailbox half-updated, and some mail stores pay an expensive open, lock, sync and close cycle for every message.
tldr.mechanism: MULTIAPPEND lets one APPEND command carry one or more messages, each with optional flags and date-time, and requires the whole operation to be atomic: either every message is appended or none is.
tldr.outcome: Clients that upload many messages get a substantial performance improvement and a clean failure mode. A server announces support with the capability name MULTIAPPEND.

today: RFC 3502 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 4466 and RFC 4469. The RFC itself says nothing further about its status.

sections.title: Uploading Many Messages at Once
sections.content:
RFC 3502 describes the MULTIAPPEND extension to the Internet Message Access Protocol (RFC 3501). It permits uploading of multiple messages with a single command. A server that supports it advertises the capability name MULTIAPPEND.

When it is combined with the LITERAL+ extension (RFC 2088), the entire upload takes a single command and response round trip. The document also states that a MULTIAPPEND APPEND operation is atomic: either all messages are successfully appended, or no messages are appended.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally you carry one letter per trip to the mailbox. This extension lets you carry the whole bag in one trip.

sections.title: Why Pipelined Appends Are Not Enough
sections.content:
In base IMAP, each message must be appended in a separate command, and there is no way to "unappend" messages if an error occurs part way. Some mail stores also need an expensive open or lock, sync, unlock and close operation as part of appending, which is costly if done per message.

A server that supports both LITERAL+ and pipelining could get some of the benefit by sending a pipelined batch of APPEND commands. The RFC gives three reasons this is weaker:

  • Multiple APPEND commands are non-atomic by definition, so there is no way to restore the mailbox if an error occurs.
  • The server may not be able to coalesce the pipelined appends to avoid the lock overhead, and any coalescing would depend on timing. With traditional UNIX mailbox files a lock is assumed to be held only for one atomic operation, and many applications disregard any lock older than 5 minutes.
  • After an error, further messages may still be appended. If a disk quota error hits the third of 5 messages, the mailbox can end up with the first, second, fourth and fifth.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending letters one after another is not the same as sending one sealed bag. If the mail slot jams on the third letter, the later ones may still slip through, and you get a mixed-up mailbox.

sections.title: The APPEND Command with Multiple Messages
sections.content:
The APPEND command takes a mailbox name and then one or more messages. Each message is given as an optional parenthesized flag list, an optional date-time string, and a message literal. The result is OK when the append completed, NO for an append error (the mailbox cannot be appended to, a problem in the flags, date-time or message text, or the append was cancelled), and BAD for an unknown command or invalid arguments.

If flags are given they SHOULD be set on the resulting message, otherwise its flag list is empty. If a date-time is given the internal date SHOULD be set to it, otherwise the current date and time is used. A zero-length message literal is an error and MUST return NO, which can be used to cancel the append.

If the append fails for any reason, including being cancelled, the mailbox MUST be restored to its state before the attempt, and no partial appending is permitted. The server MAY return an error before processing all the message arguments.

If the destination mailbox does not exist, the server MUST return an error and MUST NOT create it automatically. Unless it is certain the mailbox cannot be created, it MUST prefix the tagged NO text with the response code [TRYCREATE], hinting that the client can try CREATE and retry.

If the mailbox is currently selected, the server SHOULD notify the client immediately with an untagged EXISTS response. If it does not, the client MAY issue NOOP (or failing that, CHECK) after one or more appends. The RFC notes that APPEND is not used for message delivery, because it has no way to transfer SMTP envelope information.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand over a stack of letters, each with its own sticker and date. If any letter is bad, the post office hands the whole stack back and the mailbox stays as it was. If the mailbox does not exist, the clerk tells you to build one and try again.

sections.title: Formal Syntax Change
sections.content:
The RFC modifies the base IMAP4rev1 grammar, using ABNF (RFC 2234). The append rule now accepts one or more repetitions of a new append-message rule, which holds the optional flag list, optional date-time and the literal.

The worked example in the RFC shows an A003 APPEND to a mailbox called saved-messages with two messages. The second message follows the first one's literal on the same command, with its own flag and date-time, and the server answers with a single OK. A later example shows a NO with [TRYCREATE] for a mailbox that does not exist, and another append that fails with a disk quota error.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book used to say "one letter after the address". Now it says "one or more letters after the address".

sections.title: Interaction with UIDPLUS
sections.content:
Servers that support both MULTIAPPEND and UIDPLUS (RFC 2359) change the resp-code-apnd rule to "APPENDUID" SP nz-number SP set. The APPENDUID response code then returns as many UIDs as there were messages appended.

The UIDs returned are expected in the order the messages were appended, and the message set may not contain extraneous UIDs or the asterisk wildcard symbol.
sections.plainLanguage: If the post office hands out ticket numbers, you get back one ticket number for every letter in your stack, in the same order.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The extension raises no security considerations beyond those of base IMAP (RFC 3501). The RFC adds a reminder that IMAP4rev1 transactions, including mail data, are sent in the clear unless protection from snooping is negotiated. That can be done with STARTTLS, with privacy protection negotiated in the AUTHENTICATE command, or by some other protection mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending a bigger stack of letters does not make it any more private. Without a sealed envelope, anyone along the way could read them.

data.title: ABNF
data.code:
append          = "APPEND" SP mailbox 1*append-message

append-message  = [SP flag-list] [SP date-time] SP literal
